clinicalPearls: The commonest form of acquired ptosis, caused by age-related weakening or dehiscence of the levator aponeurosis
Features are a low upper lid margin with good levator function and a high or indistinct upper lid skin crease
In severe cases the lid can obstruct the superior visual field
It is typically bilateral but often asymmetric and gradually progressive
A key task is to distinguish it from neurogenic (third nerve, Horner) and myogenic (myasthenia, myopathy) ptosis
Levator advancement or reinsertion surgery is highly effective given the preserved muscle function
reference.pathophysiology: Involutional ptosis results from stretching, thinning or disinsertion of the levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis from the tarsal plate, an age-related degenerative change also promoted by chronic eyelid rubbing, prior surgery and contact lens use. Because the levator muscle itself remains strong, levator function is preserved, but the weakened aponeurotic attachment fails to hold the lid elevated, producing a low lid margin and elevation of the skin crease as the crease is pulled upward.
additionalDifferentials: Neurogenic ptosis (third nerve palsy, Horner syndrome)
Myogenic ptosis (myasthenia gravis, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myotonic dystrophy)
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of margin-reflex distance, levator function and lid crease position
Assessment for fatigability and other features of myasthenia
Pupil and ocular motility examination to exclude neurogenic causes
Superior visual field testing for functional impairment
Further investigation (for example acetylcholine-receptor antibodies, imaging) if a neurogenic or myogenic cause is suspected
redFlags: Ptosis with anisocoria or motility deficit suggesting third nerve palsy or Horner syndrome
Variable or fatigable ptosis suggesting myasthenia gravis
Sudden onset with pain or other neurological signs
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and progressive, and surgical repair of the aponeurosis is very effective and durable because levator function is retained.
pitfalls: Missing myasthenia gravis or a third nerve palsy masquerading as simple age-related ptosis
Overlooking coexisting dermatochalasis or brow ptosis
Attributing pseudoptosis from enophthalmos to true ptosis
Failing to document levator function before surgery
management: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude neurogenic (third nerve palsy, Horner syndrome) and myogenic (myasthenia, myopathy) causes before intervention, as their management differs
Offer levator aponeurosis advancement or reinsertion surgery as the definitive and highly effective treatment given preserved levator function
Consider a posterior Muller-muscle-conjunctival resection approach in selected patients
Manage conservatively with observation or a ptosis prop mounted on spectacles where surgery is declined or the patient is unfit
Document superior visual field impairment to establish the functional indication for repair
Address contributing factors such as chronic eyelid rubbing and contact lens wear
Monitor postoperatively for over- or under-correction, lagophthalmos and exposure keratopathy
